evidence_cards.source_context: CLIC [ 19 ] shows that imitating a set of desired actions, constructed by a pair of positive and negative actions, achieves more robust behavior than imitating only the positive action. Building on this idea, we generalize the single-step desired action set to action-chunks. At step , under observation , we denote a positive and negative action-chunk as Given and the preceding positive actions , the action is better than for all . As we consider demonstration data or intervention feedback, to make learning efficient, we adopt the approximation that being a better action than depends only on . Under this approximation, each timestep within the action-chunk yields a contrastive single-step action pair . Each such pair defines a single-step desired action set in CLIC: (8) We then define the desired action set associated with the contrastive action-chunk pair as the sequence of single-step desired action sets (9) Visualization of this set is shown in Fig. 3 (a)(b) and Fig. 2 (B1). We say an action-chunk, , belongs to this set if Action-chunks outside of this set are considered undesired. The information provided by this set can be used to train a policy, and we detail this in the following section. Figure 3: (a)(b): Visualization of the desired action set. (c): Combination of the desired action sets shown in (a) and (b).
